opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest shift I'd like to see is from agents that wait for instructions to agents that actually understand what you're trying to achieve. Right now, most agents are very good at executing a clearly specified task: you say "book this flight" or "write this function," and they do it. But in real life, people rarely give complete instructions. Humans communicate with a lot of ambiguity, and we expect the other side to fill in the gaps, ask the right questions, and sometimes even push back.

So one direction I care about is agents that can reason about intent. If the instruction is underspecified, a good agent should know when to ask a clarifying question and when to just make a reasonable assumption and move on. That's actually a hard balance. Ask too much and you're annoying; ask too little and you go off in the wrong direction. That's something we've been thinking about a lot in terms of training, because standard reinforcement learning setups tend to reward completing the task as given, not figuring out what the task really should be.

The second direction is proactiveness. A truly useful agent shouldn't only respond; it should notice things. If it's working on your codebase and sees a bug unrelated to the current task, maybe it should mention it. If it's helping you plan a trip and notices a visa issue, it should raise it before you ask. That requires the agent to have some model of the user's broader goals, not just the immediate command.

And the third piece, which is more long-term, is collaboration. I come from a multi-agent background, and I've always believed that intelligence emerges a lot from interaction, between agents, and between agents and humans. Instruction following is basically a one-way relationship: human commands, AI obeys. What I'd like is something closer to a partnership, where the agent and the human jointly figure out the problem, each contributing what they're good at.

Of course, all of this has to come with a strong sense of boundaries. Being proactive doesn't mean taking risky actions on your behalf without permission. So the real challenge is building agents that are more autonomous in their thinking, but still respectful and transparent in their actions. I think that's where the next big step for agents will be.

r001.rationale: The response describes agents moving beyond explicit commands by reasoning about intent and modeling the user’s broader goals.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention or ask about an effective memory mechanism.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, instruction following is really the floor, not the ceiling. If I tell an agent "book me a flight to Shanghai next Tuesday," and it does exactly that, fine, but a good human assistant would notice that my calendar has a meeting Tuesday morning and ask whether I meant the evening flight. That gap, between doing what was said and doing what was meant, is where I want agents to go.

Concretely, I think there are three things that have to change.

First, agents need to model intent, not just parse commands. A lot of my earlier work was in multi-agent reinforcement learning, and one thing you learn very quickly there is that the interesting behavior comes from agents that build models of other agents, what they want, what they'll do next. Right now most LLM agents treat the user as a static prompt. I'd like them to treat the user as another agent in the environment, with goals that are only partially observable, and to actively reduce that uncertainty, by asking, by inferring from context, by remembering what worked last time.

Second, they need to be able to act over long horizons and recover from mistakes. Instruction following is a one-shot thing. Real tasks are hundreds of steps, with branches, dead ends, tool failures. The agent has to be willing to form a plan, notice when the plan isn't working, and change it. That requires a kind of self-monitoring that you don't get from supervised fine-tuning on nice clean trajectories. You get it from letting the model actually try things, fail, and learn from the outcome. That's why I keep coming back to reinforcement learning, even though it's messy. It's the only paradigm that trains for consequences rather than for imitation.

Third, and this is the part people talk about less, I want agents that know the boundary of their own competence. An agent that goes beyond instructions is only useful if it also knows when not to. If it's about to delete files, or send money, or make a commitment on my behalf, I want it to stop and check, even if I didn't explicitly tell it to. Autonomy and calibration have to grow together. Otherwise you just get a more confident way of being wrong.

So when I say "beyond instruction following," I don't mean agents that ignore you. I mean agents that understand you well enough that you don't have to spell everything out, that can carry a task across days and tools and setbacks, and that have good judgment about when to come back and ask. That combination, I think, is what makes something feel like a collaborator rather than a very fast intern.

r001.rationale: The response proposes agents infer user goals from context and remember what worked before, so they can act beyond explicit instructions.

r002.rationale: It mentions remembering what worked last time, but does not ask whether agents could have an effective memory mechanism.

astra-6.text:
I’d like agents to move from following individual instructions to understanding the goal behind them. If I ask an agent to help with a research project, I don’t want to specify every search, every experiment, and every next step. I want it to make a plan, notice when something isn’t working, and adjust.

But taking initiative also requires knowing when to ask. An agent should be able to say, “I can do this, but there’s a tradeoff here—what matters more to you?” The interesting challenge is giving agents enough independence to be useful while keeping people able to understand and steer what they’re doing.

r001.rationale: The response describes understanding goals and taking initiative beyond individual instructions, but does not raise the possibility of personalizing agents to individual users.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention or ask about an effective memory mechanism.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d like agents to move from simply executing commands to understanding what we’re trying to accomplish. If I give an agent a task, it should be able to notice missing information, ask a useful question, and propose a better approach when my instructions don’t quite serve my goal.

That also requires judgment about when to act and when to check with us. For something reversible, it can take initiative and learn from feedback. For a consequential decision, it should make its assumptions clear and ask. The goal is a collaborator that helps us think and act more effectively, while leaving us in control.

r001.rationale: The response describes understanding goals, asking questions, and adapting to feedback, but does not clearly raise the possibility of agents becoming personalized.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention memory or ask whether agents could have an effective memory mechanism.
